title: From Table to Tower
premise: You start with one wooden table in a busy Nigerian market and a ₦50,000 thrift payout. Shop by shop, truck by truck, you build a family group that feeds, banks, houses, teaches, heals, flies and powers the country. Every new company exists because an older one needed it. The top is not a bigger shop: it is a tower with your family name on it and a market that still knows you.

hero.howPlayerAppears: Player-made founder, any gender, about 22 at the start. Begins in slippers and an apron; clothes, car and house change with each act, and the hair goes grey by Act 6.

family.name: Mama Ireti Adeyemi
family.role: Taught you the trade. Gives the evening-at-home advice and one small daily goal; her pride meter is the story score.

family.name: Tobenna
family.role: Your first manager. Later runs the group in trust while you serve in local government, so nothing stops earning.

family.name: Zainab Lawal
family.role: Keeps the books. Warns three days before salaries and tax fall due and explains every new money system simply.

family.name: Alhaji Musa Garba
family.role: Old trader who runs the thrift circle that funds your first table. Opens each act with a challenge and a story.

family.name: Papa Okon Bassey
family.role: Holds the family farmland in the village. Visiting him unlocks the farm supply link and the yearly homecoming event.

acts.name: One Table, One Dream
acts.story: Alhaji Musa's thrift circle pays out ₦50,000 and Mama Ireti gives you her old table. You choose one trade, carry every load yourself, hire your first helper and grow the stall into a proper shop. By the end the whole row knows your name and Tobenna asks for a job.
acts.newSystem: The core loop: collect, process, sell, upgrade pads, five venue stages, first staff and the evening routine at home.
acts.travel: On foot and by keke inside one city: the market, the supplier yard and home.

acts.name: Owner of the Row
acts.story: One shop becomes three and suppliers cannot keep up. A late truck spoils a week of stock, so you buy your own van. Good staff are scarce, so you open a small training centre behind the shop. Papa Okon invites you home to see the farmland. You stop being a trader and become an employer.
acts.newSystem: Second and third market shops, managers, monthly salaries and tax, and the first supply links between your own businesses.
acts.travel: By car to nearby cities and the family village to visit suppliers, the farm and your first branches.

acts.name: City Money
acts.story: Traders on your row still keep cash under the mattress, so you open a small licensed bank for them. Rent keeps rising, so you start building your own shops. Imported goods cost too much, so you make them here. Zainab draws all of it on one page and Alhaji Musa says: now it is a group.
acts.newSystem: The holding company screen: one page for every business, internal loans, transfers and a monthly owner dividend.
acts.travel: Domestic flights between Lagos, Abuja, Kano and Port Harcourt for licences, land and factory sites.

acts.name: A Name in Nigeria
acts.story: You are always on the road, so you build hotels you would sleep in. A staff emergency shows the town needs a hospital. An app puts your bank in every pocket and a film makes the brand famous. Then neighbours ask you to serve at the council, and Tobenna takes the keys while you do.
acts.newSystem: Reputation: a national fame and trust score that lifts customers everywhere, plus the family trust for time spent in public office.
acts.travel: Weekly domestic flights across all regions, plus car tours of your ward and the towns you serve.

acts.name: Across Africa
acts.story: Your goods now cross borders and prices swing with every currency. A trading desk steadies them, an investment bank raises big money openly from the public, and when flight delays cost you a deal in Nairobi you start an airline. The girl or boy from the row now signs in five capitals.
acts.newSystem: Markets and currency: export prices move daily, the group can hedge, issue bonds and list shares on the exchange.
acts.travel: International flights to Accra, Abidjan, Nairobi, Johannesburg and Cairo; free once the airline flies there.

acts.name: The Tower
acts.story: Every company you own pays too much for power, so the last and biggest build is energy: gas, solar and a grid that keeps the lights on at home. The group opens offices in London, Dubai and Guangzhou and moves into its own tower. From the top floor you can still see the market row.
acts.newSystem: Legacy: train an heir, fund a foundation, and unlock the Next Generation prestige run.
acts.travel: Long-haul flights to London, Dubai, Guangzhou and Houston, by your own airline or private jet.

holdingCompany.name: Table and Tower Group
holdingCompany.howItWorks: Unlocks in Act 3 as a boardroom screen. Each business is one card showing cash, profit per hour, manager and a health light. Drag cash from a rich card to a hungry one as an internal loan at 5% interest. On the last day of each month the group pays salaries and tax first, then sends 20% of what is left to the owner's pocket as dividend. Red lights mean a visit is due.

synergies.bonus: Own-farm supply cuts raw goods cost in the kitchen by 20% and removes the supplier delay.
Farm loans at 9% a year instead of 25% from outside lenders; a harvest loan doubles one season's planting.
Own containers lift fabric export profit by 30% and trucks return full, saving 15% on shop restock.
Graduates start at skill level 3 instead of 1 and cost 25% less to hire.
Own-brand goods on the shelf earn 35% more margin than bought-in stock.
Building in-house cuts hotel construction cost by 25% and build time by 2 days.
Staff health cover cuts sick days by 40%, so stations stay staffed.
The mobile app triples new customers per day and lets 50% of shop sales be paid by transfer.
Flight-and-room bundles raise hotel occupancy by 20%; owner trips cost ₦0 on own routes.
Own power cuts factory running cost by 30% and ends blackout stoppages.

travelLoop: Each business has a health light that drifts from green to red over about 7 days without a visit. A trip takes 2 to 4 minutes: pick the city, ride or fly, walk the site, fix 3 small problems, greet the manager and sign one deal only the owner can sign. Never travel and red sites lose 5% output a day down to half, managers stall and new licences, land and partners stay locked.
prestige: At the top you name an heir and endow a foundation. Next Generation starts the heir with one table in a new city (Kano, Accra, Nairobi) under new rules. You keep the tower, house, family album and Legacy Stars: each adds 10% to all earnings. Seasonal city leagues and events keep running.
weeklyRhythm: Daily: collect overnight earnings, clear Mama Ireti's goal and run the flagship by hand for a few minutes.
Twice a week: take one trip to the reddest site, fix three problems and sign an owner-only deal.
Midweek: open the group screen and move spare cash to the business that is next to upgrade.
Friday: the market-day event doubles customers for one hour in a featured business.
Weekend: play the story chapter Alhaji Musa sets and claim the act milestone reward.
Month end (every 7 real days): pay salaries and tax, read Zainab's report, collect the dividend.
toneGuide: The player is the hero; family and staff are guides. Celebrate effort before money.
Warm and funny, never mocking. Light Pidgin in dialogue only; menus stay in plain English.
Clean wins only: fraud, bribes and tax dodging are problems to fix, never shortcuts.
No tribe, religion or party jokes. Invented names only; real cities are fine.
Keep the market in sight: every act calls back to the first table and the people on the row.

research.claim: Idle games base prestige currency on lifetime or since-reset earnings, and one common cube-root formula means about 8 times the earnings are needed to double the prestige reward.
A 2025 tycoon design review calls monotony the core problem of the genre, says 'no events, no game', and warns that new gameplay layers must be introduced gradually so newcomers are not overwhelmed.
A Lagos couple grew from 50 bags of cement taken on supplier credit into building materials, supermarkets and filling stations, opening the fuel arm because of the group's own fuel spending.
In the same group, trucks that deliver cement return carrying supermarket stock, and cash from the pay-before-delivery arm funds expansion of the others, coordinated at group level.

A Nnewi spare-parts trader moved from trading to local assembly and then vehicle manufacturing, building his own plastics and tyre companies to secure inputs instead of buying them at others' margins.
